summary: Guidance for separating route-level quotas to protect low-latency streaming from high-throughput embedding jobs
description: BrightLedger reports repeated 429 errors on their low-latency streaming endpoints during periods when downstream ingestion jobs (embeddings) run at high throughput. They want prescriptive guidance and example configuration for: 1) guaranteeing low-latency streams are not throttled by high-throughput batch jobs, 2) recommended route-level quota settings, and 3) a migration plan from current tenant-wide quotas to route-isolated quotas without downtime. Customer indicates they are on enterprise tier and can use dedicated pool if recommended.
steps_to_reproduce: Customer runs continuous streaming workload to gptx-7b-stream endpoint (websocket-based) from 50 concurrent clients.
Every 10 minutes, a batch embedding job kicks off to text-embedding-ada-002 with 200 parallel workers for 45 seconds.
During the 45s embedding window, some streaming clients receive 429s and experience resumed connection backoff despite low per-client QPS.
Customer observes X-RateLimit headers showing remaining tokens drop to 0 for the streaming route during the batch job window.
logs: Customer-provided snippet: 'most streaming sessions are very short (50-200ms) and our embedding workers open short-lived parallel connections.'
investigation_notes: Initial hypothesis: tenant-wide token accounting allows embeddings to consume shared refill budget causing temporary depletion for streaming route.
Observed pattern: spike in token consumption aligned with embedding job windows; streaming route sees immediate hit because tenant bucket is drained first when route-level isolation is not enabled.
Quota engine supports per-route isolation and burst-capacity; customer is currently on tenant-only quotas (no per-route override).
Risk: naive per-route limits set too low could cause 'shadow throttling' for bulk workloads; conversely, too high per-route limits defeat isolation goal.
Alternative: dedicate a capacity pool for embeddings (Dedicated) to fully isolate noise; tradeoff is cost/commitment.
proposed_resolution: - Configure a per-route soft quota for streaming route with higher priority and a small guaranteed burst reserve. Example CLI: redwood quota set --route /v1/streams/generate --guarantee 2000 --burst 5000 --priority high
- Add a routing policy that sends embedding traffic to a separate route name (e.g., /v1/embeddings/high-throughput) so quotas can be separated cleanly.

- Enable per-route quota isolation in Console: create 'streams' route group with 'isolate=true' and set sustained and burst parameters. Create 'embeddings' route group with separate sustained/burst profile and lower priority.

- If acceptable, provision Dedicated pool for embeddings and configure routing policy to prefer dedicated pool for 'embeddings' route. This guarantees that embeddings cannot draw from streaming pool's tokens.
- Use token-window smoothing: set refill_window=10s for the streaming route to avoid minute-aligned refill sawtooth behavior for short sessions.
- Add transparent throttle headers and enable rate-limit-decay-logs for 48h to validate behavior after change.

1) Create route groups in staging and replay production traffic for 2 hours. 2) Enable 'isolate' and set conservative sustained_capacity equal to 80% of recent 95th percentile for each route. 3) Monitor rate-limit headers and Console per-route dashboards. 4) If stable, roll to prod with 15-minute canary window. 5) Optionally move embeddings to a Dedicated pool after validation.

- Recommend clients respect X-RateLimit-Reset and implement jittered exponential backoff for ephemeral short sessions.  Short streams should prefer connection reuse (HTTP/2) where feasible to avoid repeated token accounting for connection initiation.
